articles.title: Christian Nationalism
articles.author: H. Scott Prosterman
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The political tsunami that brought new blood to the U.S. House and Senate also set in motion a fresh dialectic to challenge the nativist Christian Nationalist movement in the U.S. While U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has been a forceful “Christian Soldier” in promoting illegal Christian and Jewish settlements in the West Bank, Texas Senator-Elect James Talarico is one of the newly elected officials poised to re-direct that narrative. Convicted felon Donald Trump has benefitted from his alliance with white Christian nationalists, who perceive him as a modern-day King Cyrus , a powerful heathen sent by God on their behalf. Though Trump has shown to be the most unspiritual man to sit in the Oval Office, they bought his con because he also appeals to their sense of nativism, racism and exclusion. African-American politicians such as the Rev. Ralph Warnock (D-GA) in the Democratic Party have long appealed to a sense of Christian justice, and the late President Jimmy Carter famously combined his Baptist faith with center-left positions. Still, this fall’s crop of preacher-representatives on the Democratic side of the aisle are remarkable. Related: Trump’s Executive Order 13899: Jewish Identity, Free Speech, and Palestinian Rights. Now come seminarians such as Talarico, Kansas Senator-Elect Adam Hamilton, and Texas Congressman-Elect Frederick Douglass Haynes III with historic upset wins. Their political strength comes in part from their objections to the MAGA Christian Nationalist agenda, and its misapplication to justify Israeli colonialism. The movement that empowered Trump, and fueled the January 6 riots is now being challenged by Christians who “walk the walk,” rather than those who twist the teachings of Jesus into instruments of hate. The strength of Talarico, Hamilton and Haynes comes from their calling out how Evangelical Christianity has been misinterpreted to promote Trump’s very un-Christian agenda. Whereas Trump’s army of Christian soldiers violently stormed the Capitol to disrupt the electoral process, claiming divine empowerment; Pastor Haynes began his campaign by stating that Jesus opposed genocide in Gaza and anywhere in the world. Trump’s Christian soldiers are as devoted to the sanctity of firearms as they are to Jesus. The new wave of “walk the walk” Christian Democrats are positioned to challenge that position. Their election brings a welcome “ Christian counterpoint to the evangelical support for Israel that has long dominated the religious debate over the U.S.-Israel relationship.” They are deploying the momentum of the Blue Tsunami to counter that reflexive support for the Zionist enterprise and to reclaim modern Christianity for the actual teachings of the New Testament. The warped invocation of Jesus in Trump’s project has been a destructive force in American society, religion and politics. Anyone not invested in MAGA welcomes the new liberation theologians in the House and Senate. Though all three of the figures mentioned above take exception to various Israeli military actions, there are subtle but notable differences in their approaches. Let’s examine their theological and political backgrounds, which led to this historical moment. Talarico has been a vocal critic of Christian Nationalism, and called it “a cancer on our religion.” Though he studied at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary, he was never ordained. Talarico been a forceful advocate of economic justice, separation of church and state, and public education free of religious influence. He also opposes book bans, and supports affordable childcare and paid family leave. He opposes U.S. sales of offensive weapons to Israel, but supports Israel’s right to defend itself from Iran and other enemies. Talarico advocates disarming Hamas and a two-state solution that recognizes Israeli and Palestinian sovereignty. But he opposes the unlawful Israeli squatter-settlements, and their ongoing expansion. Informed Comment

articles.title: Outsourcing War
articles.author: John P. Ruehl
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The election was a major setback for Trump and the MAGA party. But still, our Republic is in danger. The Project 2025 Christian Nationalist crowd continue to run the administration. And with the appointment of the fanatical Stephen Miller as chief of staff, Trump appears to be doubling down. Moreover, with his suspected cognitive decline, he may pose an even greater threat to the social order that our nation and Western allies have enjoyed for generations. Other powers seek to destroy our Republic. Trump’s best friend Vladimir Putin despises America for its principles and its support of Ukraine’s fight for independence and democracy. And internally, players like Elon Musk and Peter Thiel scorn democratic governance, which they view as inefficient and obsolete. They supported Trump’s autocratic ambitions. Musk alone poured half a billion dollars into the midterm elections backing Republican candidates who blindly support Trump’s goals. Related: Are Billionaire Politicians Becoming the New Normal? Peter Thiel is a Silicon Valley technocrat with a net worth of $37.7 billion . He is not a showman, like Musk, but is as dangerous. Here is his view of government : “I think it is only a small exaggeration to say that the government is so fundamentally evil that to deny the evil nature of the government is equal to denying the existence of the devil… I think it is better for us try to do something noble than to spend the rest of our lives trying to make compromises with the base.” What could be more un-American than the idea that government “of the people, by the people, and for the people” is evil and that compromise, which is the essence of democracy, is less than noble. Thiel, a mentor to JD Vance, fueled Vance’s rapid rise in government. He invested $15 million in Vance’s Ohio senate campaign and arranged Vance’s introduction to Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago where he smoothed over Vance’s earlier criticism of Trump, which ultimately led to his selection as Vice President. Vance share’s Thiel’s philosophy of government. Thiel and Musk believe government should be run like a corporation, i.e., under a CEO. Rather than an elected president, the CEO would be appointed, ostensibly by a board composed of oligarch technocrats. Both Musk and Thiel advocate stripping away federal regulations and civil service protections, arguing that the state should operate with the lean efficiency and speed of a Silicon Valley startup. This ideology was evident in Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which utilized corporate tactics—like mass workforce reductions and executive orders—to bypass traditional bureaucratic checks and balances. Did Musk’s DOGE enterprise cut costs? No t even close to what Musk claimed it did, and far less than the $2 trillion he initially claimed it would. He wiped out the USAID Agency. And look at the consequences. The Center for Infectious Disease Research at the University of Minnesota estimates that 750,000 lives have been lost and a UCLA Fielding School of Public Health researcher finds that cuts may lead to more than 14 million additional deaths globally by 2030—the Theil-Musk ideology in action. Related: The Business of AI Fear: Who Profits From Doomsday Hype? This simplistic philosophy fails in two essential ways: it lacks values. Good governance requires a moral foundation, not just efficiency. it lacks purpose. A government should exist to serve the common good, not merely to cut costs, especially as Trump claims the US economy is stronger than ever. The effectiveness of a government cannot be measured solely in economic terms. Its performance must be judged against its founding principles. A CEO in charge of government is no different than a dictator. There are few instances in history where a benevolent dictator served to advance the common good. Benign autocrats are rare, and the lack of accountability inherently risks corruption, systemic oppression, and catastrophic failure, making democracy far more resilient, as demonstrated by America’s 250-year history. The Thiel-Musk philosophy is, at best, wildly optimistic in the short term and doomed to failure in the long term. Accountability Musk must be held accountable. His interference with Ukraine’s access to the Starshield military satellite system, operated under his direction, must be investigated. Trump and Musk blame each other for aiding Russia, but a decision with such consequences should never have been made without democratic accountability. Ukraine’s struggle parallels America’s fight for independence in 1776, and so the public overwhelmingly supports Ukraine’s cause. Musk’s DOGE sabotage of USAID, an agency established by Congress, must also be investigated. Created in 1961 by President Kennedy, it was formally codified by Congress as an independent agency in 1998. Can this, or any administration, simply dissolve an agency so established? There are reasons against a third impeachment of Donald Trump. The earlier failed attempts served to divide the nation and drew attention away from other urgent matters that faced congress. And Republican gaslighting made those attempts appear as political revenge. But accountability, justice, and the rule of law are far more important than motivation. Yet pundits are already asking Democratic leaders, will you seek revenge? The question they should be asking is, will you seek justice? Related: Migrants Are Not the Weapon, Governments Are One must consider Trump’s access to America’s most confidential information in the context of his close relationship with Vladimir Putin and his admiration for other autocratic leaders. With his flagrant dishonesty and lack of respect for our Constitution, he simply cannot be trusted to act in the nation’s interest. The danger Trump poses to our national security is real. He should be removed from office. Impeachment appears to be the best solution. Sixty-seven senate votes are necessary. When all the votes are counted, Democrats will likely have fifty-six. There just may be eleven Republicans who care enough about national security to remove him from office. Democrats, a party for the people? There must be consequences for those who violate our Constitution and laws. Democrats have a responsibility to ensure that justice is served. But Democrats need to do more. They must demonstrate that they are for the people. An October Gallup Poll reported that only 43% of U.S. adults view the Democratic Party favorably. And the party must reckon with the fact that Americans chose Trump and his MAGA supporters in two elections. Trump won because people are dissatisfied with the political system the favors wealth and corporations; dissatisfied with the system that shifted eighty trillion dollars from the bottom 90% to the top one percent between 1975 and 2023. On average that is $247,000 for everyone in the bottom 90%, which is 60% greater than their average net worth ($153,000). Unquestionably, American government has favored the wealthy. Democrats and Republicans alike share responsibility. Trump promised change but failed to deliver. To regain the public confidence, Democrats must deliver; make government work for the common good. If they fail to address the sources of public dissatisfaction, resentment and distrust will continue to grow and fester. Changing our economic system so that wealth generated by economic and technical progress benefits the common good rather than the wealthy alone is a monumental task. As AI eliminates both white and blue-collar jobs, the present means of allotting income by salaries and wages and taxing that income will soon become obsolete. Related: America and Russia: Why a 250-Year Rivalry Never Found Its Footing We must find new methods of compensation and taxation that distribute economic gains fairly. Without change, wealth inequality will continue to grow, threatening the stability of our economic system. The current course is unsustainable. The Republican party no longer has the wherewithal to address problems of this nature. Democrats must lead the way. This article was produced by Economy for All , a project of the Independent Media Institute.

articles.title: Revolution and Fun in France - YDSA
articles.content: France’s ongoing student uprisings have featured music, aura battles, combativeness and joyous celebration. To build a socialist movement in the US, we need to understand our biggest material barriers to revolutionary joy. “J’ai deux passions: la fanfare, la révolution” I have two passions: the marching band, the revolution “Vive les blocages, les sabotages” Long live the blockades, the sabotages “Les ZAD et les manifs sauvages!” The ZADs and the riots! -French Protest Anthem Protestors in costume (left) facing off with riot police (right), (October 31st, Wikimedia Commons ) Over the past two months, workers and youth have risen up across Europe , with their agitation spreading to parts of South America, Asia , and even Canada . While it is not the aim of this article, nor within its scope, to discuss the implications of these events for the young socialist movement here in the United States, the demonstrations from France offer one very important takeaway: They are having fun. This may sound like an insignificant detail, but if we want to achieve mass mobilization on a similar scale in our own communities, and if we want to go beyond the energy of our previous rebellions, then we have to understand why we are currently materially unable to . So let’s look into the revolutionary joy of the masses in France – through chants and bands, aura and militancy – as well as how we can get to their level ourselves. Good Chants and Music The rain sprinkles onto Place de la République . You stand, surrounded on all sides by a sea of your comrades, waiting in anticipation. Then, it begins – trumpets, drums, violins, cymbals, all a wall of noise – but this isn’t any ordinary concert. It’s playing songs reminiscent of long battles, drawing from your community’s decades-long history of struggle. Bella Ciao . The Internationale . Even some pop-culture rebel music from Star Wars and The Hunger Games. A new crowd favorite, J’ai Deux Passions , brings everyone into chorus: One of the most defining features of the protests in France was this abundance of wonderful noise. Not only have there been creative chants, but there’s been whole bands and orchestras out on the streets, in the squares, and they’ve even spread to Spain . The ability to have mass, collective participation in music stems from the united, revolutionary base of the multiracial French working-class – where amidst this diverse proletariat, everyone’s on the same page, with common interest and solidarity in the face of repression. This can be contrasted with the examples of reformist, white, and liberal No Kings protesters here in the United States, who in many places just walked down the street and chatted to themselves or stayed silent, maybe doing one or two half-hearted call-and-responses. Aura Masked demonstrator strikes a pose in front of a burning dumpster (October 17th, Instagram) The aura of an uprising can come from a variety of sources. As previously mentioned, you can start a chant or play an instrument. You can get on top of something and wave a flag. You can take photos in front of some burning stuff. You can look out and see thousands of people with you, all marching as one. Or, you can have an aura battle . Aura battles and their predecessors, dance and rap battles, have been around for decades under various names. In France, they’ve been one of the biggest ways working-class kids have begun their political involvement these last few months. This is because aura battles are a youth cultural practice that, though at first non-political, are a form of collective organization that can lead into political work. Just like socialists in 19th-century Germany pieced together a working-class sport and art culture , so too have young revolutionaries in France pieced together their working-class culture by providing an organizing infrastructure for collective activities like aura battles, music, and more. As young socialists in the US, we should look to intervene in our own youth and working-class culture, using joy and solidarity as a deterrent against both reactionary social behaviors and as a tactic of revolutionary organization. Militancy One of the biggest things that makes taking to the street fun is becoming unstoppable. Those of us who were around during the George Floyd Uprising, or during certain high-intensity pro-Palestine and anti-ICE struggles in the years following, know the thrill of having a protest “pop off”. We take the streets, become a force, and don’t let anyone stop us. Every day we spend fearful of, and in submission to the cops makes moments like these feel that much better. Young protestors atop the Monument à la République in Paris (October 17th, Wikimedia Commons ) In France, much like the US in 2020, youth and students have held the line, forced police to retreat, and asserted their power despite repression by the brutalizing, heavy-handed CRS (French National Police) . Their boldness has imbued the movement with a revolutionary character and has exploded the contradiction between the workers and the capitalist state. Now let me make this clear before you get any ideas: militancy must be born OF the people, not imposed upon them. If we jump the gun and act recklessly, or take a commandist approach over the movement, we risk alienating ourselves from our communities. We also risk becoming walking targets for an incredibly repressive judicial system , and causing harm to those we are trying to protect. We’ll get to the fun stuff when the workers have built an organizing infrastructure and movement that can support it. Why Not Here? The reason that France, Europe, and parts of South America are in revolt while we’re stuck either watching from the sidelines or being preoccupied with “fixing the system from within” isn’t due to any metaphysical difference between us and them – it’s due to our material conditions. The fragmentation and atomization of the proletariat and the breakdown of our basic socialization processes, especially in the years following the Covid-19 Pandemic, have been the primary contributors to our lack of joyous revolutionary struggle. We can’t simply rely on broad analysis, apparently easy answers, or smooth-talking populist politicians – we should take seriously the horror that this question implies: Why have we stopped playing in our moments where liberation seems possible? On another note, Y/DSA and other left-wing organizations, as they exist today, are often composed not of the multiracial proletariat, but rather the white downwardly-mobile petit-bourgeoise or “middle class” . Radicalized by the rapidly-declining benefits of life in the imperial core, these college-educated workers form the basis for a movement which, while good-intentioned, often inadvertently seeks to restore their benefits looted from the Global South and internal colonies. The Medicare for All, College for All, Green New Deal, and Tax the Rich campaigns generally exemplify this tendency . DSA 2021 Member Survey Report ( 2021 ) If we want to be like the French youth and achieve revolutionary joy through uprising, we must work to develop a revolutionary struggle that seeks to destroy the capitalist state itself, not just ask it to be nicer to us. YDSA members should attempt to support the organization of non-white and non-student youth, who both make up a majority of 18-24 year-olds, in their workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods. Only by addressing the crisis of proletarian disorganization can it become possible to rise up en masse against our capitalist enemies. Always remember that we are beginners — we have so much to learn and so many ways to grow as socialists. In the struggle for a better and dare I say more France-like world, the best time to get started was yesterday, the second best time is now! Manny Heffley “Revolt” graffiti from George Floyd Uprising (2020, Unknown )

articles.title: Trump's Economic Fantasy
articles.author: Julianne Malveaux, PhD
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In his run-up to the midterm elections, the president is crisscrossing the country in an effort to energize his base. Unfortunately, he seeks to inflame his base with multiple exaggerations, obfuscations, half-truths, and downright bald-faced lies. Thus, he told Oklahoma’s News 9 on October 1, “So we have the greatest economy in the history of our country.” The data says otherwise. Consider the September employment report, released October 2. The economy added just 29,000 jobs. Earlier estimates for July and August were revised downward by a combined 60,000. July, initially reported as a month of job growth, now shows a loss of 10,000 jobs. These numbers hardly support the president’s extravagant celebration. Related: The Census Is a Ledger of Power The overall unemployment rate was 4.2 percent, a relatively low figure. But whose unemployment are we discussing? Black unemployment rose from 6 percent in August to 7 percent in September. White unemployment was 3.6 percent. Black workers were unemployed at nearly twice the rate of white workers. Monthly figures fluctuate, particularly for smaller demographic groups. One month should not carry an entire argument. Yet the familiar racial disparity deserves scrutiny every month. When politicians celebrate the national unemployment rate while overlooking Black unemployment, they erase people whose economic circumstances complicate their preferred story. A presidential declaration does not pay the grocery bill. It does not fill a gas tank, cover the rent, or produce a job for someone who has been looking for months. And a national economic average tells us precious little about the distance between those enjoying prosperity and those struggling to survive. What does a “strong economy” mean to the worker whose application goes unanswered? What does it mean to the family drawing down savings while waiting for a paycheck? Losing employment can mean losing health coverage, falling behind on housing payments, and postponing an education. For households with little accumulated wealth, unemployment can turn a manageable budget into an emergency. On October 5, the national average price of regular gasoline was approximately $4.37 a gallon. In Washington, DC, it was about $4.45. Nationally, filling a 15-gallon tank cost roughly $65. Retail diesel averaged $6.32 a gallon, adding pressure to businesses that move food, equipment, and other necessities. Prices had eased over the preceding week, but a modest decline does not make an expensive tank affordable, nor is it acceptable when precipitously higher year-over-year from 2025 . Ask a farmer about this supposedly magnificent economy. John Boyd Jr., president of the National Black Farmers Association, told NPR in September that filling his tractor cost roughly $1,000. He was paying about $7 a gallon for diesel, nearly twice what he paid a year earlier. “This is a national farm crisis for farmers,” he said. USDA projects farm fuel and oil expenses will rise nearly 29 percent this year. For Black farmers, whose operations are generally smaller and whose access to credit is more limited, another surge in operating costs can threaten both a livelihood and the land that sustains it. You cannot harvest a crop with a presidential boast. Related: Republicans Had Project 2025: Where Is the Democrats' Plan? Trump’s October 5 diesel order offers an election-season promise of relief, with - crucial details left to Treasury. It directs officials to pursue tax deferrals for highway use of off-road diesel, not guaranteed tax forgiveness. Tractor fuel already receives tax-exempt treatment. Farmers hauling crops may benefit, but postponing taxes does not solve high fuel prices. The latest inflation report, for August, tells a story families know from their ballooning bills. Overall prices were up 3.4 percent from a year earlier, but energy prices jumped 16.3 percent. Gasoline surged 27.4 percent, and home heating oil soared 52 percent - a punishing increase as winter approaches. Groceries, electricity, and shelter also cost more. This is the president’s “greatest economy?,” families paying more for the necessities they cannot do without?! These increases arrive on top of prices families already found difficult to manage. Slower inflation does not restore yesterday’s purchasing power. It means prices are rising more slowly. People waiting for their old grocery budget to buy their old grocery basket understand the distinction. An economy can expand while leaving millions financially insecure. Investors may celebrate rising asset values while renters wonder how to renew a lease. A household with substantial savings can absorb higher fuel costs. A household counting dollars until payday has fewer choices. Economic growth matters, but so does its distribution. If the president wants credit for prosperity, then he should answer questions about who receives it. Where are the opportunities for workers excluded from the celebration? What is being done to close the racial employment gap? How are families supposed to manage the cumulative increases in their basic expenses? Voters should ask these questions of every candidate seeking their support. They should demand specifics about employment, wages, housing, transportation, and the ability to build savings. Campaign enthusiasm is no substitute for economic security. Related: Public Austerity Becomes Private Debt Calling this the greatest economy in our history is an invitation to examine the evidence. That evidence includes weak hiring, persistent racial disparities, and household expenses that continue to climb. The president can keep repeating his false superlatives, while families still have to figure out how to pay their rising bills. The question persists: A strong economy for whom? BlackCommentator

articles.title: Climate Revolution
articles.author: Marcus Baram
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Almost no one ran on climate change this fall, but the election may reshape climate policy all the same. Democrats won both houses of Congress, a majority of governorships and — as projected by the National Conference of State Legislatures — control of 25 state legislatures by talking about prices: gasoline, diesel, home heating and above all — electricity. Geoff Garin, a Democratic pollster who works with the advocacy group Climate Power, told Capital & Main that nearly three-quarters of Democratic candidates in battleground-state races ran at least one ad about energy costs. “The old Republican mantras of ‘drill, baby, drill’ and American energy dominance were and are wholly irrelevant to the current energy debate,” Garin said. “Instead, the energy debate now is focused on [President Donald] Trump’s ill-conceived war, on data centers, on price gouging by oil companies and on Trump’s war on clean energy.” Indeed, in a NBC News exit poll , 74% of voters pointed to the war in Iran as a major factor in their vote and 86% said they were concerned about utility costs. In Garin’s polling , 53% said producing more wind and solar power would make energy more affordable — with one in five saying renewables would make it much more affordable. Voters who rank climate first in their priorities, meanwhile, showed up early. Across the 21 states where the nonprofit Environmental Voter Project works, 49.3% of its identified climate voters cast early ballots, said Nathaniel Stinnett, the group’s founder. That was up from 41% in the 2024 presidential election and 32.5% in the 2022 midterms, he told Capital & Main. “Even if politicians weren’t talking about climate, climate voters were sure thinking about politics, because they ran to the polls to vote as soon as possible,” Stinnett said. “I think we can safely say that the climate crisis is already impacting our political choices and behavior in a profound way.” In Washington, the answer over the next two years is oversight and leverage but little new law. In state capitals and town halls, it could be a great deal more. Washington: Subpoenas, spending and one live bill Neither Democratic majority approaches the two-thirds needed to override a veto, and Trump has promised to use his freely. David Victor, a professor of public policy at the University of California, San Diego, predicted a stalemate at the federal level. That leaves three tools. The first is the gavel. Starting in January, Democratic chairs in the House reportedly plan to use subpoena power to investigate budget cuts, staff reductions and pollution-limit reversals at the Environmental Protection Agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin. They also plan to examine deals in which energy companies traded offshore wind leases for fossil fuel development or won exemptions from Clean Air Act requirements. Related: Russell Vought's Federal Grant Plan Raises Questions About Executive Power The second is the purse. Democrats intend to use must-pass spending bills — broad budget bills required to finance federal agencies, military operations, national parks and public services — to restore money for climate research, disaster resilience and clean energy grants. They also may try to revive clean energy tax credits repealed in the 2025 reconciliation law, framing them as a way to cut utility bills. A Senate majority can also block nominees to the EPA, the Energy Department and the federal bench. The third is the one major bill that’s actually already moving. The Senate voted 73-25 on Nov. 9 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, designed to speed reviews of power plants, transmission lines and data centers. Democrats are split. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, voted no, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has voiced his opposition. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), in line to chair the House Committee on Natural Resources, wants amendments that would shield clean energy projects from agency discrimination, end federal buyouts of offshore wind leases and make data centers pay for their own power needs. “Voters sent a clear message last week that they want better deals than the ones they’ve gotten under unified Republican leadership,” said Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the environment committee who won reelection in the midterms. Democrats, he said, owe voters a deal “that delivers clean energy megawatts and jobs, near- and long-term savings on energy bills, and real climate benefits without leaving so many important members of our community on the losing side of the ledger.” The oil and gas industry has a different take on the election results. Mike Sommers, chief executive of the American Petroleum Institute, said the affordability message was unmistakable and called the permitting bill the place for bipartisan cooperation to start. The White House said Trump remained committed to reliable, affordable and secure energy. However, the incoming class of Democrats is not of one mind. U.S. Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas promised to protect oil and gas jobs. Rep.-elect Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) framed climate change as a “national security crisis” and called for federal investment in solar, wind and geothermal power and a return to the Paris climate agreement. Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, a 36-year-old co-founder of the climate advocacy group Sunrise Movement who won a swing seat in Michigan, campaigned for state and federal moratoriums on hyperscale data centers — and, as Grist reported , has moved away from the Green New Deal’s massive build-out toward the politics of community control over projects and clean energy. The states: Six new trifectas The most immediate changes are expected where Democrats won the governor’s office and both legislative chambers: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. The party also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Pennsylvania has the biggest runway. Democrats flipped the state Senate to cement the first trifecta since 1993, and lawmakers plan to pass long-stalled bills streamlining community solar, warehouse solar and battery storage while barring local governments from banning renewable projects. Gov. Josh Shapiro, who has presidential aspirations, has also proposed a carbon cap-and-trade program, which sets a hard cap on emissions, similar to what California and other states have on the books. Related: Starbucks Gets a Tax Break: Families Pick Up the Tab In Michigan and Minnesota, restored trifectas are likely to protect laws requiring 100% clean electricity by 2040 from repeal and open the door to grid modernization bills. In Arizona and Wisconsin, new majorities could pursue the renewable standards and decarbonization targets that Republican legislatures blocked for years. Utility regulators are shifting too. Democrats won both open seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission for a 3-2 majority, their first majority in decades, and new appointments in Michigan and Arizona are expected to bring tougher scrutiny of utility spending on fossil fuels. Michigan voters went further, approving a measure that bars state-regulated utilities such as DTE Energy from contributing to the campaigns of officials who oversee them. The bill was backed by U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. A separate measure to replace DTE Energy with a public utility was narrowly defeated. Local: The data center revolt Closer to home, the story was almost entirely data centers. Voters in 10 states decided 41 local measures, 21 of them in Ohio, and 32 with reported results favoring limits. Pataskala and Granville, Ohio, approved bans on facilities above 25 megawatts with 74% and 82% of the vote. Newly elected local officials in states such as in Pennsylvania and Virginia campaigned on the same promise — reining in data centers. They are expected to tighten zoning, require new facilities to procure their own renewable power and keep utilities from passing grid upgrade costs on to residential ratepayers. Not every local measure said no. Voters in Eugene, Oregon, approved a Clean Energy Fund that places a 2% license fee on large retailers such as Amazon and Walmart to pay for renewable energy and job training. It is expected to raise at least $15 million a year by 2030 and was modeled on Portland’s 2018 fund, which has invested $1.7 billion. Related: Trump's Coal Revival Is Raising Electric Bills—and Voters Are Fighting Back The local votes set up the next fight. Pennsylvania Democrats want to stop towns from banning solar farms even as towns across the Midwest vote to ban data centers — and legislatures weighing statewide rules will have to decide whether to codify those bans or override them. Garin, the Democratic pollster, said the politics favored his side. Each of those issues, he said, “gave Democrats the high ground in the energy debate, and I think that that will continue to be the case as we move from elections into legislating and policymaking.” Capital & Main

articles.title: Los Angeles Socialists Won Big in the Blue Electoral Wave
articles.author: Chris Kutalik
articles.content: LA was at a critical cusp in its history. Globalization had reorganized its economy, rewiring it in dramatic ways, and many people were being left behind. Yet the city had — and still has — this incredible, protean potential for better things, for progressive politics, for surprising activism. — Mike Davis, 2006 The midterm elections were truly seismic. Like many places across the country, Los Angeles made good on its protean potential from the 2026 blowout with a stronger socialist movement and a larger share of political power. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members won up and down the ballot. Nithya Raman won the mayor’s office of the country’s second-largest city in an upset victory. Marissa Roy has won the city attorney’s office, and Angela Gonzales-Torres is headed to Congress. Together their victories put democratic socialists in two of Los Angeles’s most powerful citywide offices and sent a DSA-LA member to Congress for the very first time in a race that few expected a year ago would even be a close challenge. The formerly conservative, sleepy suburb of Burbank has elected a DSA council majority, one of the first on the West Coast. Behind those wins is DSA’s second-largest chapter. In the last year alone, the LA chapter doubled its membership to over six thousand members, launched a citywide Shake Up LA slate, and knocked more than 110,000 doors. And it did so alongside a realignment of the city’s left-labor coalition, especially that of the powerful hotel workers union UNITE HERE Local 11, which cross-endorsed most of DSA-LA’s Shake Up City Hall slate from Nithya down to Burbank City Council, and whose thousands of members knocked doors for her. National Earthquake This didn’t happen in a vacuum. Nationally, Democratic candidates of all stripes won control of both chambers of Congress, while Republicans lost ground in a shocking 99 percent of roughly 2,100 counties where most ballots had been counted by the morning after the election, according to Reuters. The electorate shifted left nearly everywhere, all at once. Within that national revolt, Los Angeles voters were also shifting left. Gonzales-Torres decisively defeated Democratic incumbent Jimmy Gomez, winning over 62 percent of the vote while running openly as a DSA member, supporting a free Palestine and the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and rejecting corporate money. Her victory gives DSA-LA its first foothold in Congress with a candidate that took clear positions against corporate power and state violence and for Palestine and the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement while building a winning electoral coalition. Roy’s victory carries a historic mandate as well. With more than 695,000 votes and roughly 68 percent support, she received the largest vote total ever won in a Los Angeles city election at any time, according to her campaign. She campaigned uphill, against the Democratic establishment and real estate lobby’s support of the incumbent, on turning the City Attorney’s Office into LA’s largest public-interest law office: pursuing abusive corporate landlords, enforcing workers’ rights, holding polluters accountable, and challenging the Trump administration in court. LA Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, in an official portrait from 2022. (City of Los Angeles) Raman’s mayoral victory expands that opening considerably. Her 2020 city council victory helped establish DSA-LA as a force in city politics. Six years later, she has defeated incumbent (and onetime New Leftist) Karen Bass to become Los Angeles’s first democratic socialist (and immigrant) mayor. Her victory gives the socialist movement a new scale of power to advance housing, tenant protections, and public services across Los Angeles. An ongoing tension will be between her independence as an elected and the co-governance and criticism of both the LA chapter and DSA’s national leadership about her level of support for the BDS movement and other issues she may not be in lockstep with the chapter on. The chapter has also consolidated its existing beachhead on the LA City Council. City Council Members Eunisses Hernandez and Hugo Soto-Martínez and Los Angeles Unified School District Board Member Rocío Rivas all won reelection. In the Inglewood area, Estefany Castañeda retained her seat on the Centinela Valley Union High School District board, while Yaritza Gonzalez won election to the Inglewood Unified School District board. Red Burbank The chapter’s reach also expanded beyond Los Angeles. In Burbank, victories for Mike Van Gorder and Nolan Southerland created a democratic socialist council majority alongside Konstantine Anthony, while Stephen Post won in West Hollywood . Estuardo Mazariegos’s race in Los Angeles’s Ninth Council District remained unresolved, with Mazariegos trailing by a mere eighty-seven votes after taking on an opponent backed by major corporate and police union spending. Los Angeles is also part of a national advance forward by socialists. DSA reported at least eight members elected to the next House: Gonzales-Torres, Chris Rabb, Darializa Avila-Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Claire Valdez, and Donavan McKinney, alongside Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Rashida Tlaib. Its election coverage also recorded state legislative wins in Florida and Tennessee. These wins give the socialist movement more opportunities to connect local organizing with struggles over national policy. The scale of the work behind these campaigns matters. In its largest electoral effort to date, DSA-LA endorsed thirteen candidates and mobilized more than 1,700 volunteers to fill over 4,000 canvassing shifts. Its members knocked more than 110,000 doors in chapter-led canvasses. Over the same period since the 2024 election cycle, membership grew from nearly 3,000 to more than 6,000 and has added several hundred new members since Election Day alone. The Long Arc The chapter’s program places this strategy in a longer history of multiracial working-class struggle, from Justice for Janitors in the 1990s to the immigrant rights marches of 2006 and the teachers’ strike of 2019. Those movements demonstrated how organized workers could reshape Los Angeles’s politics and advance demands benefiting the wider public. A DSA-LA member at a May Day 2026 rally. (DSA Los Angeles) Combining electoral work, movement activism (from anti-ICE mobilizations to mass transit organizing to Palestine solidarity work), and member growth points toward a way to build durable socialist organization and power. An endorsement backed by thousands of volunteer shifts creates opportunities to develop new organizers and leaders, forge relationships with neighbors, and bring people into a member-run organization. Keeping that capacity alive takes work. New members need meaningful roles and on-ramps to activity, political education, and a voice in deciding what comes next. Campaign volunteers need opportunities to remain active after their candidate wins or loses. There is a wide constituency for that work. Gallup’s September report found that 43 percent of Americans viewed socialism positively , the highest share in its series. In Los Angeles, late October University of California, Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies polling put democratic socialist identification at roughly a third of likely city voters. “The democratic socialist constituency is real, and it is growing,” said DSA-LA Cochairs Leslie Chang and Sean Wakasa. The Promise The election results alone cannot settle every argument about which message or strategy worked best. They do, however, create an opening for a Left that offers more victories, confronts concentrated wealth, and refuses to sacrifice solidarity for supposed electoral advantage. The next test will be whether these victories open up more struggles and, most of all, change people’s lives. Roy’s promised enforcement agenda, a stronger socialist presence on city council, and Raman’s incoming mayoral administration create opportunities. Those gains, as always, will require organized pressure, alliances with unions and community groups, and members willing to remain involved in the difficult work of governing. They will also take sustained and coordinated pushing and accountability from movements and DSA locally. The promise of the democratic road to socialism is that working people can collectively govern the institutions that shape their lives. In Los Angeles, that promise now has more members, more organizers, and more elected socialists behind it. articles.title: The Enshittification of Everyday Life
articles.author: Jatinder Hayre
articles.content: Have you tried to speak to a human being lately? Perhaps you wanted to question an energy bill, rearrange a hospital appointment, claim a benefit, or discover why your insurer had refused treatment your doctor said you needed. You will probably have been invited to download an app, create an account, and remember a password. The most recent demand is that you must interrogate a chatbot. And then, as a final act of administrative penance, you can telephone a call center, where a recorded voice assures you that your call is terribly important. Somewhere along the way, a strange inversion occurred: the institution still takes your money, increasingly so, but you perform more and more of the labor. This sort of scenario is usually called decline, but I think that is too generous. Decline suggests something tired, neglected, perhaps capable of rescue with another budget, or, more rarely, a sufficiently earnest politician. What we have instead is a deliberate paradigm shift. Cory Doctorow has a gloriously apt vulgarity for this: enshittification . Digital platforms court users with convenience, become indispensable, then worsen the bargain once leaving becomes harder than staying. You can delete Facebook. Try deleting your need for health care. Privatization and austerity have produced a miserable chimera: monopoly capitalism married to managerial bureaucracy. Government commissions, contractors deliver, regulators regulate, consultants advise, managers manage. Together they form the processariat : everybody owns a part of the process; nobody quite owns the responsibility. The exhausted receptionist absorbs the anger, while staffing and spending decisions are made in the ivory tower. Meanwhile, you are still on hold. This is “socialized inconvenience.” Once, institutions encountered complexity and employed people to deal with it; now they email the complexity to you. We photograph the meter, chase the referral, upload the evidence, and pursue which department has lost the form. Nevertheless, this is recorded as efficiency. Even the language has been enshittified: a closed desk becomes “digital transformation” and work transferred from salaried staff to unpaid customers becomes “empowerment.” Still, enshittification is subtler than collapse: things keep functioning, but with enough friction to render using them a second occupation. Your Call Is Important to Us As a practicing doctor, I see the more dangerous version. Being ill is work nobody pays you for: ringing at the right hour, decoding the letter, affording the fare, losing a day’s wages, explaining yourself again to somebody new. Patients increasingly become project managers of their own illnesses. The sicker the patient, the more administrative competence we seem to demand of them. The sickest people are often required to become the most capable bureaucrats. I remember one of my own patients who underwent a biopsy of a neck lump and was found to have cancer. The biopsy was performed, the pathology was reported and the result entered the system. Yet no appointment followed, no clinician called and nobody appeared to take responsibility for what happened next. My patient simply waited, assuming that somebody, somewhere, was dealing with it. Of course, cancer does not wait to consider mitigating circumstances. On paper, each step had occurred. In reality, the one thing that mattered had not: the patient had not been followed up with. Every part of the process can function while the person at the center of it is still failed. The American version comes with insurance paperwork. In a survey of 4,155 insured adults ages eighteen to sixty-four, 24.4 percent reported delaying or forgoing care because of administrative tasks. Respondents with disabilities reported greater burdens; those with higher incomes, fewer. They already had insurance. The affluent can often buy their way out of the processariat altogether: a private consultation instead of the appointment queue, a taxi instead of the disrupted train, a tutor instead of navigating a struggling school, an accountant or assistant instead of another afternoon lost to forms and hold music. Those without that option remain trapped inside the machinery and pay in the resource institutions almost never count: time. Forty minutes on hold is an irritation to somebody answering emails from home — to a care worker on an unpaid lunch break, it can mean abandoning the problem altogether. Money increasingly buys something subtler than luxury — an exit from process. In 2024, across twenty-eight OECD countries , the poorest fifth were, on average, 2.5 times more likely than the richest fifth to report unmet medical needs because of cost, distance, or waiting times. Chasing down a child’s appointment or a parent’s prescription requires human effort. The International Labour Organization’s 2018 report , drawing on sixty-four countries, estimated 16.4 billion hours of unpaid care work daily. Women performed 76.2 percent. Institutions shedding work rely on households already doing plenty. We empirically tested whether the effort and resources an intervention requires affect who benefits from it. Income support, housing measures and regulation produced the most consistent equity gains. Programs demanding sustained personal effort, without support, often widened health inequality. Giving everybody the same instructions does not give everybody the same capacity to act on them. When people give up asking, that can look like reduced demand, although the need has gone nowhere. Please Rate Your Health From One to Ten Arkansas made Medicaid coverage conditional on work and reporting requirements. By the time a judge halted the policy, eighteen thousand adults had lost coverage . Researchers found no employment increase over eighteen months. In Jharkhand, India, reforms introducing biometric identification for subsidized food reduced corruption, but an estimated 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point during the reforms. The researchers traced much of the harm to how the transition was managed. Public ownership must mean enough staff with the authority to resolve problems. Universal entitlements must be obtainable without a second occupation spent pursuing them. The worker answering from another country has no more power over the staffing budget than the patient waiting. Both have an interest in changing who controls the service. And an institution claiming an efficiency saving should have to account for the work transferred to the public. Perhaps the most corrosive achievement of enshittification is our own habituation. We budget for the delay, expect the missed call and quietly absorb another piece of work the institution once did for us. What begins as irritation becomes adaptation. What once looked like failure is the new baseline. The processariat wins twice: first by making the service worse and then by persuading us that expecting better is somehow unreasonable. As we wait, chase, upload, appeal and telephone, the processariat can point to its dashboards and insist that the machinery is working. Broken institutions would at least have the decency to stop. Enshittified institutions keep going, largely because we have been conscripted into keeping them going ourselves. But at what cost?
