articles.title: What the ’60s Left Gave Us
articles.author: Adolph Reed
articles.content: Before the Bernie Sanders presidential runs, the last big upsurge in radical American politics occurred in the 1960s. This moment is remembered for its civil rights activism and student antiwar protests, but how should we really understand the New Left’s rise and fall? On this latest episode of the Jacobin Radio podcast Confronting Capitalism , Vivek Chibber and Melissa Naschek are joined by political scientist and longtime socialist organizer Adolph Reed Jr for a wide-ranging conversation about the ’60s radicals. They look at the rise of the student movement, the developments in postwar Marxism, and the birth of modern identity politics. Confronting Capitalism with Vivek Chibber is produced by Catalyst: A Journal of Theory and Strategy and published by Jacobin . You can listen to the full episode here . Melissa Naschek Today we’re going to focus on the New Left and its legacy, specifically regarding race and identity politics. To start us out, Adolph, can you talk about how you became involved in politics and what your involvement in the New Left was like? Adolph Reed Yeah, it’s pretty prosaic. I was nineteen when Stokely Carmichael shouted black power in the Meredith March . I had already been politically aware, not just because I was precocious but also because of my family. However, I hadn’t been especially active until then. I was at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill in 1966, and it was the crest of a period of intense campus activism and right on the edge of the beginning of another one. And like a lot of people in my demographic, the black power slogan was quite cathartic and effective. In addition, the first big escalation of the Vietnam War had occurred the previous summer in 1965, and I already had friends who had been drafted, gone over, and been killed within a two month span. The antiwar movement was kicking off on campus and I got involved in that. I was also involved with protests against the local Community Action Program. In a kind of a no-person’s-land between Chapel Hill and Carrboro, the Community Action Program decided to use funds to develop a neighborhood cleanup and beautification campaign on the principle that poor people were poor not because they didn’t have enough money, but because they were demoralized and needed a more beautiful environment, with flowers and stuff. Melissa Naschek This sounds like a prelude to broken windows. Adolph Reed Yeah, it absolutely was. So some of my friends and I started protesting the stuff that they were doing. On top of that, I did some voting rights work and some tutorial work through an organization called Youth Education Services, YES. At Chapel Hill, programs like that and other sort of do-gooder stuff worked through the campus Young Women’s Christian Association or YES, which became like a magnet for young people looking to be active in politics. And much of the leadership of the student left and even the Pan-African post-student left crowd had gone through YES in one way or another. But both the tutorial experience and voter registration drive were pretty formative for me. Melissa Naschek For those who don’t know, the Community Action Program was a program initiated by the 1964 Economic Opportunity Act passed by President Lyndon Johnson as part of his War on Poverty programs, which aimed to take federal dollars, invest in communities in some way, and leave it to the communities to combat poverty on their own terms. But you’re also talking about your political activism after the Voting Rights Act, which was aimed at getting more people involved in the political system . Adolph Reed Exactly. I think the voter registration campaign came first. At the time, the old seniority system in Congress was still in effect, so the strategy was to target the newly enfranchised black voters to vote against the incumbents who had been there for forever, had a lot of seniority, and controlled party politics. In one of these elections, there was a challenger named Jim Gardner, the owner of the first Hardee’s franchise, up against an incumbent Democrat named Harold Cooley, who was also horrible. And we were supposed to register people to go vote against Cooley by voting for this Goldwaterite Republican, who, if he won, wouldn’t have any seniority. So I did it and was knocking on people’s doors. I know this sounds like a cliché, but you know, I’d seen a lot of poverty in my life, but I’d never seen that kind of poverty before. This was worse than sharecropper’s shacks. I mean open sewage, kids outside with sores all over them, flies the size of B-52s. And after a couple of days of doing that, I thought, “Look, there’s no way I can in good conscience sell these people on the idea that they need to register to go vote for this one guy against the other one.” That was a disillusionment that led me to my father’s politics, basically. So I did that and the tutoring for as long as I could until a group of black power radicals took over the campus NAACP chapter and I was part of that. And then there were a couple of labor actions over in Greensboro. The state AFL-CIO would recruit us to go walk the picket lines at the Cone Mills corporation and that’s how I got drawn into the labor movement . Understanding the New Left Melissa Naschek I think what’s so interesting and compelling about your career is that you came out of political work and then later went into academia to study politics. When I read your work, it’s clear how those experiences really shaped how you analyze and understand political developments. But let’s take a step back and look at the broader picture. When and what was the New Left? Adolph Reed There are narrower and broader ways to delimit what they were. First of all, there was a New Left that originated in the UK, principally during the 1950s. That emerged basically from a critical tendency within and around the Communist Party (CP). There was also something kind of comparable in the United States in the 1950s, which formed around journals like Studies on the Left and figures like C. Wright Mills and Dwight Macdonald. Some were Trotskyists or former Trotskyists. Vivek Chibber But much smaller. Much of the first generation of British New Leftists came out of the Communist Party, as Adolph said, and they saw themselves still as more or less Marxists. They believed the Communist Party had strayed and moved away from a vision of socialism. This was the generation of E. P. Thompson, Eric Hobsbawm, and other people around them, although Hobsbawm never left the Communist Party. In the United States, the New Left came from outside the CP, such as people like C. Wright Mills, as well as the precursors to Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), with the influence of Herbert Marcuse and people around him. And so it is a lot smaller in the United States, because the Soviet invasion of Hungary was a big catalyst in the UK, as well as Joseph Stalin’s death and the 20th Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. These all had a very big impact over there. But you would know more, Adolph. It seems to me less so over here, right? Adolph Reed I think that’s right. I think it was much less so, and what drove the cultural-intellectual space here that was the equivalent of the New Left there was something more like what Russell Jacoby romanticizes in The Last Intellectuals . So the combination of the continuing movement of the Trotskyist element from City College in the 1930s, as they were moving toward the National Endowment for Democracy and the right wing, basically, to becoming neoconservatives. By and large, people often said they were looking for “a non-communist left,” but what they just as likely meant was “a non-Marxist left.” Melissa Naschek What’s the distinction there between a non-communist versus a non-Marxist left? Adolph Reed Well, there’s a lot of tiptoeing wordplay around all these politics, and in the last two or three years I’ve come to feel that most of the time when Americans talk about an “anti-Stalinist Left,” what they’re really trying to distance themselves from is Marxism . And that was not necessarily the case in the UK. But in the United States, there were people like Macdonald, Mills, the liberal Partisan Review crowd, as well as Michael Harrington, the author of The Other America and the founder of one of the parents that produced the Democratic Socialists of America ( DSA ), the Democratic Socialist Organizing Committee, and the Dissent group led by Irving Howe. All of these individuals were militantly anti-communist and combined a literary high intellectuality with a liberal sort of semi–social democratic left edge of the Democratic Party politics. What became the Students for Democratic Society, created in 1962, had originated out of the League for Industrial Democracy. And the original name, in fact, was the Student League for Industrial Democracy, but then somebody read the acronym and thought they needed to do something else — that’s not the best name, and they were always kind of a funny amalgam. For the American left in the 1950s and ’60s, there was no real class politics that defined it. This was a period in the United States when people didn’t even talk about capitalism or class . I mean, one of the unfortunate contributions of our tribe of social scientists to the hegemonic ideology was inventing the notion that the old ideological distinctions like capitalism and communism don’t make any sense anymore, and what we have now is industrial society. And Vivek’s discipline, quite like mine, from one angle was predominantly characterized by trying to make capitalism and class disappear. Vivek Chibber I would say, all the way through the late 1960s, postwar sociology was fundamentally backward. And it’s returning to those roots now. Adolph Reed So I’ve noticed. Vivek Chibber One of the ways in which the British and the American New Left differed is that there was a similar intellectual move away from talking about capitalism in England, but that comes out of the Labour Party. This was called revisionism within the Labour Party and was led by Anthony Crosland. And he tried to make the argument that capitalism had evolved to the point where we can think realistically about actually maneuvering beyond its class contradictions and managing it in what he would call a social democratic or egalitarian direction. This would have meant that capitalism’s defining qualities, what Karl Marx called its laws of motion, are now a thing of the past. That was an argument coming out of a section of the Labour Party. There was, of course, another very class-oriented and socialist section of the Labour Party that resisted this. In the United States, there was a kind of working-class-oriented section of the New Left as it was forming both inside the Students for a Democratic Society and outside. But very little of it was Marxist. It was pro-labor, but it didn’t really have a theory, and that’s why you had that famous speech by Paul Potter where he said, “We have to name the system.” And this was considered a controversial statement, right? Very little of it was Marxist, and they didn’t really have a theory about the system that they were challenging. This is much less so in England, because that New Left was much more imbricated within Marxism. It had a real connection to the labor movement as well. So we can say that the British New Left was trying to reform Marxism, whereas the American New Left was stumbling toward “discovering it,” and that’s the way I’ve always understood it. And the American New Left really didn’t have that much of a connection to labor until later. I think in the late 1960s or early ’70s, there was a big move toward labor inside the student-based left organizations, which was called “industrialization” back then, but that’s ten to twelve years into the biography of the New Left. Adolph Reed Yes, absolutely. A few years ago, I reread what may be considered SDS’s manifesto, the “Port Huron statement,” and I was struck at how much the authors of that statement had internalized all the postindustrial and post-ideological stuff. Classes disappeared from the analysis. They were as concerned as any op-ed writer in The New York Times about the problems of an affluent society and how to deal with abundance , and they were by and large people who came out of working-class families — union families, even. Radical Goals and Politics Melissa Naschek So what were the most clearly articulated political goals of the New Left? Adolph Reed Well, one was a demand for racial justice. It wasn’t exactly clear what that would would mean concretely. Another was of course to end the war. So neither one of those was derived from a model of how the society could be different from the way it is now and could be improved, which is what you would typically think of as the vantage point of an avant-garde. Another goal, of course, was personal expression, and if you want to talk about the roots of identity politics, well, bingo. And I have memories of meetings that lasted all night long because of the principle that every voice should be heard. Melissa Naschek We’re talking about the period from the 1950s to the ’60s, so are there different time points at which the main political priorities of the New Left evolved? Adolph Reed Yeah, I think that’s right. SDS’s roots were also in the early direct-action phase of the civil rights movement. A number of the founders had already been involved in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. But there were also a lot of prefigurative politics or a commitment to a prefigurative ideology. Melissa Naschek Can you explain what that means? Adolph Reed Well, for people who can remember, it’s like Occupy Wall Street , to the extent to which people who participated in occupations generally understood themselves to be embodying what the ideal society should be and will be , and that they were enacting the society that they wanted to see. That’s what prefigurative politics comes down to, and it’s a principle that has its roots in theology, that the way to make the world you want is through something like a demonstration effect from inside your organization. Vivek Chibber So you create in the organization a microcosm of what you want to see outside the organization. It sounds really nice or a great thing to do, depending on what your vision is of what an organization should be trying to do and to be. But consider a trade union. Ultimately, a trade union is a fighting organization. What you want to do in the trade union is have the meeting, make a decision, and then move on. But if it turns out that your vision is that everybody has to have a voice, you don’t leave until everybody said something, and you turn it into something very different from what the function of the organization is. And so a lot of organizations are killed around these principles. Adolph Reed And ironically, that’s one of the things that really took off and became a bigger and bigger problem once the New Leftists had approximated something called Marxism. And I’ve got personal stories I can share about this. Melissa Naschek I think hearing those would be helpful to make this a little bit more concrete. Adolph Reed This one is a little bit of a shaggy-dog story: I left college in the spring of 1969 after a cafeteria strike and was trying to figure out what to do. There was a guy who had been involved in setting up a couple of the first GI antiwar coffee houses, one at Fort Hood in Texas and one at Fort Jackson in South Carolina, and he started talking about the idea of doing one at Fort Bragg. So I decided to do that. But before I went down there, I went up to Fort Dix, where there was a coffee house mainly funded by people who had formed an organizing collective and were all living in a big, unheated farmhouse outside Wrightstown. The principal male in the group was coupled up with the most conventionally attractive woman in the group. And they were committed to destroying capitalism cellularly, right? I mean, not at the workplace. Vivek Chibber One café at a time. Adolph Reed Right. He was acting out a Mick Jagger thing, like chopping wood in the cold with no shirt on and firing off weapons. But on my second day, he told me that there was a Black Panther coming over from Jersey City to meet with him at the office and he wanted me to go with him. So I did. I had read that Bayard Rustin quip that there were only like a thousand members of the Black Panthers and half of them were cops — and that’s mainly the experience I had with Panthers , especially by then and especially on the East Coast. But during our meeting, our principal male — I’d literally never seen anything like this in my life before — his entire demeanor and body language changed. He kept scratching his arms, he was inarticulate in the face of the Panther, and the Panther was playing it for all his worth. In this group, there was also a former Vista worker and a former Catholic seminarian who set himself up as the psychotherapy guru. I didn’t quite realize that Maoist self-criticism could be articulated in that way, but he was basically holding confessions for everybody else on his staff. I thought, “This is nuts.” But this is really the point of this: I eventually figured out that the movement into co-ops and organizing collectives tended to deteriorate to that kind of psychologistic pathology because they weren’t able to organize. So, that fraction of the Left came to Marxism at the point when the ruling class had already basically won in 1960s. Vivek Chibber It’s interesting that you bring up Marxism here, Adolph. One of the things that stands out to me is that, whatever its foibles and whatever its initial confusion around how you understand the system and where you go, after the first ten or twelve years, that student left ends up stumbling into Marxism for the most part. And the reason is that, if you called yourself a radical in the 1960s, and even into the ’70s, radicalism was socialism, and socialism was Marxism. It was still the case back then. And so, whatever else there was in the ether, Marxism was still the self-identified hegemonic theory of the Left. That’s what’s so different from today. What’s different today is that you call yourself a radical, and the last place you go is Marxism. Because what’s called radicalism now has morphed into all these various sort of avatars of the crap that you’re talking about, which has to do with personal politics, personal perfection, psychologism, and most of all, the class commitments and aspirations of the elites and professional groups within blacks, women, among immigrants, all whom have taken taken over the rhetoric of radicalism. So what you have now is a radicalism that combines this personal perfection, self-help safety-ism, masked-forever kind of confessional culture on the one hand, which is a direct descendant of that student left, but with something genuinely new on the other, which is that there’s never been a time in the history of the Left when you actually made it a point to denigrate the socialist and Marxist tradition while calling yourself a radical in the name of, and in the pursuit of, professional bourgeois aspirations. Students and Workers Melissa Naschek What was the New Left’s attitude toward the working class? Did it engage in working-class organizing? Adolph Reed Yeah, some did. But there were different tendencies. So I mentioned that when I first got involved in activist stuff, one of the first things that I and others got connected with was going to walk the picket lines for the textile workers. And there was no daylight between doing the anti-poverty stuff that we did or the anti-anti-poverty stuff we did or even the voting rights stuff we did. Everybody was doing the same kind of work, and everybody understood that the working class was the center of our activity. And then that changed gradually. The summer of 1967 was the “Summer of Love” or something like that, and that’s when you really started to get the counterculture line coming to dominate the movement. That’s when you began to see people who didn’t approach politics as an organizing project, but who approached it much more as a domain of self-expression and a display of your consumer habits and stuff like that. And that’s when you get that gloss on “The personal is political,” which was of course not the perspective that came out of the Waveland conference that gave birth to the second wave of the women’s movement. I think about even the early representations of the 1960s version of the New Left in popular culture. They were banalized in the typical way. It was all reduced to fashion and smoking weed or whatever and being free. And that’s part of what drove the massive influx into SDS after 1967. The first thing that came to my mind when I heard DSA had exploded in membership was what happened to SDS: there was a flood of emotionally powered and earnest people that came into the organization with no particular politics, and by the end of 1969, it didn’t exist anymore. Vivek Chibber It is interesting that of the student organizations, the socialists who came out of Trotskyism and Maoism both made a decision to dive into class organizing, right? And it was the International Socialists, the IS, that created Teamsters for a Democratic Union, which continues today. It’s still around, and it played an absolutely pivotal role in the Teamsters and in organizing them. But the unfortunate experience of the Maoists was that they went into the auto sector right at the time when all the layoffs started, and so they found themselves kind of holding the bag. So both of these tendencies existed at the time. On the one hand, what Adolph is talking about, with the flower children and the counterculture and consumption habits. But then I think there was a very serious component of that student left as well, mainly because it came to Marxism, and because there was an oral tradition that was still alive coming out of the 1930s and ’40s Old Left which transmitted to them the importance of class organizing, the trade union movement, and immersing themselves in it. You can see glimmerings today of a return to class organizing within the DSA. It’s now called salting, whereas back then it was called industrializing. So there is a kind of salting component of the DSA , but also all of those strands that Adolph is talking about in the 1960s inside Students for a Democratic Society can be seen today. But in my opinion, the weightage is now reversed. Today’s Left is far more dominated by the personalistic, identitarian self-help therapy thing, and the class component is now struggling to find its bearings. Adolph Reed When we were working on the Labor Party in the 1990s, one of the things that really struck me was how common people in the intermediate level of trade union leadership had come out of those sectarian Marxist groups. And it makes perfect sense to me: I mean, you do that work for a while, and you learn how to organize, and you learn what what makes sense and what doesn’t practically, but you keep the politics and you keep the goal. And from the ruling-class standpoint, it’s interesting that among the leadership of three of the major international unions in the country, until the merger stuff happened, included a president who graduated from Yale, a president who graduated from Cornell, and a president who graduated from Penn. And by the early 1970s, people at the business roundtable were already complaining that there weren’t going to be class-appropriate jobs to absorb all these people who are going to college, and all keeping access open would do is produce an adversary culture. Anti-Imperialism Renewed Melissa Naschek How do you two think the Vietnam War and the antiwar movement impacted the relationship between the New Left and the working class? Adolph Reed Well, there’s a standard story and then there’s reality. The standard story is that the working class was patriotic and for the war. But see, the people who were telling us this were the same people from Vivek’s discipline and mine who had been “inventing” the working class as tautologically male, conservative, and Catholic. They basically invoked the same idea as Ronald Reagan’s image of Joe Six-Pack. But Penny Lewis at the City University of New York wrote a great book called Hardhats, Hippies, and Hawks that challenged this story. What she found was that, at every point during the Vietnam War going back to Dwight D. Eisenhower, support for the war increased with education and income. So the hard-hat thing was a stunt, basically. But this makes perfect sense, because whose kids were getting drafted, right? So this is another part of a concocted fantasy that the Democrats were recomposing an alliance by packaging a right-wing foreign policy as though it appealed to the concerns of the working class. Vivek Chibber Within the student left, the war had a dual effect, one positive and one negative. The positive one was that the war really brought the importance of imperialism into the culture of the student movement. And because a lot of the students were coming to Marxism, it took them back to the theory of imperialism in order to try to develop an account of how the Vietnam War was emblematic of or a departure from the imperial role that the United States had played in the postwar global economy. This brought them to the question: What was postwar imperialism, and to what extent was Vladimir Lenin’s theory adequate to the task of understanding it? Among those who took this up were individuals like Anwar Shaikh , who just passed away . Anwar was in large measure motivated to redevelop Marxist economics so that it could be a foundation for developing a theory of international capitalism and, potentially, imperialism. There was a deadly seriousness to this. And to my mind, the Vietnam War played a very large role in the revitalization of Marxist economics among the students, and that was very positive. But then I think there was also a negative side to the Vietnam War’s impact on the student movement. Both because of when it occurred and because of the centrality of Maoism inside the student movement; it also revived what is called “Third-Worldism.” Third-Worldism was the idea that the Western working class had essentially been bought off and corrupted by the fruits of imperialism. And so accordingly, not only was their general wealth derived from this, but they had a direct material stake in the superexploitation of workers in the Global South. This made them, at best, a kind of uninterested party in fighting imperialism, but at worst, a reactionary mass. Arghiri Emmanuel, in his very influential book, Unequal Exchange , says explicitly that workers in the West don’t just benefit from imperialism, but they exploit workers in the Global South. That thinking led, I think, to a fairly negative and dismissive attitude toward class organizing domestically, as well as an exoticization and valorization of anything happening in the Global South as the only thing that actually matters. In my opinion, this led to much of the American left conceptualizing the Global South in a profoundly reactionary way. Since after all, workers were now being called exploiters of countries in the Global South, the countries as a whole in the Global North were said to benefit from and exploit countries as a whole in the Global South. Ironically, this theorization ended up making the American left the organic intellectuals of the Third-World bourgeoisie. Because all the most backward and reactionary nationalist programs and policies in the Global South were now seen as effectuating the agency of these so-called darker nations. So, there is a quite striking legacy that comes out of the 1960s, which I believe has become hegemonic on the student left today, which exoticizes and essentializes the cultures and nations of the Global South and refuses to acknowledge that there are profound class divisions in those countries. The truth is that the first enemy of the workers in most of those countries is not American workers or even multinationals coming out of America, but their own immediate exploiters, their capitalist classes. That’s unfortunately a very debilitating legacy of that period, which was roundly criticized by the Left in the 1970s and ’80s both here and in the Global South. But because of the intervening years, with the death of Marxist political economy and class analysis, I think one big reason it’s been revived today is that it converges with the kind of identitarian race discourse we have in this country, so that it’s easily slotted into saying “whiter people in whiter nations dominate darker nations.” It’s made out to be a component of global white supremacy or something like that. Adolph Reed Yeah, I think that’s absolutely correct. So after Vietnam won the war, many left-inclined liberals in particular came to feel betrayed when it turned out that the Vietnam Workers Party wanted to build a state. Because what they’d always had in the back of their minds were these noble peasants. Vivek Chibber In my view, many of these leftists think of the people in the Global South as zoo animals. Adolph Reed Yeah, that’s exactly right. Vivek Chibber To be pitied, to be petted, but never to be recognized as basically the same as you. This reminds me of what Bayard Rustin said regarding the black middle class . He said that the white left has to understand that the black middle class is like any other middle class, and it’s going to do exactly what they do, which is craft a narrow agenda for itself and try to palm it off as a people’s agenda. Adolph Reed Totally. And during the 1990s anti-globalization movement, I remember debates after a South Asian economist wrote a fiery op-ed piece in the Times about how it was racist to attempt to regulate child labor. And what stunned me was that us lefties actually tried to debate among ourselves about whether we needed to acquiesce to this guy’s understanding. And I said, “What’s his job? What’s his title? Brother, who do you think he works for?” This type of thinking has been a continuous problem and it’s still around. Vivek Chibber It rears its head whenever issues of imperialism or empire come up, and there’s still unfortunately a big chunk of the Left, including inside the DSA, that has the view that the welfare state was built on the fruits of empire, that the white American working class is benefiting from it. What’s interesting to me is they insist on equating the Western working class with white working class, because, if you really believe that empire is what sustains the West, then black workers are as liable in the brutal exploitation of these Bangladeshis as the white ones are. You don’t really hear this implication very much because it’s all a racialized discourse. ’60s Counterculture and New Politics Melissa Naschek What was the relationship like between the New Left and the counterculture? Adolph Reed It varied a lot. On one hand, I rarely met a drug I didn’t like back then. In fact, as I reflect on it, I can hardly think of one now. But on the other hand, and I can still produce some witnesses to this too, I had no use for countercultural politics at all, and quickly came to see those people as an obstruction. Melissa Naschek Yeah, and when you say countercultural politics, what do you mean? Adolph Reed This is basically what’s called lifestyle politics. As well as the notion that there was a youth culture and something called the youth movement, which I also can produce witnesses to attest that I didn’t believe in then, when I would have been in a position to benefit from it actuarially. There was the “Age of Aquarius” stuff, the idea that there was a new consciousness that emerged in society that has to do with generational change and the new perspectives. And that flowed very naturally into the New Politics tendency within the Democratic Party. Melissa Naschek Can you explain what that was? Adolph Reed The New Politics tendency emerged from a combination of aspirant blacks, latinos, women, and environmentalists who were jockeying for organizational leadership positions within the Democratic Party. They tended to be post-class-oriented in identifying the problems, seeing Americans as consumers rather than as producers or as workers . And that tension played out around the George McGovern campaign between the Vietnam War and the Johnson administration. Lyndon Johnson’s identification with the New Deal , at least rhetorically, saddled the New Deal coalition more broadly with the baggage of the war. There was a fetishized disparagement of George Meany [the leader of the AFL-CIO], who was in fact pro-war but also tarred as a racist. The way these condensation symbols work is there’s some effective zephyr that’s there for anybody who wants to connect with. It was never directly theorized, and so there wasn’t really space to have a debate. The other national status politician who was directly associated with the New Deal and horrible racism was Mayor Richard Daley in Chicago, and his authorization of the police riot against antiwar protesters at the 1968 Democratic convention. It also fueled this untheorized notion of “us versus them,” and on a purely moral basis. Over the 1970s, Jimmy Carter became a crucial actor in this. Carter ran for governor as a candidate of segregationist nostalgia and rose to national visibility at the 1972 convention in Miami as the organic head of the Stop McGovern movement. His number one sidekick in that was a black state legislator from Atlanta named Ben Brown, who would become chair of Carter’s campaign and then later the Democratic National Committee. When Carter ran for the presidency for the first time, he billed himself on his fiscal probity and boasted about how many government departments he had cut when he was governor of Georgia. For that reason, as well as others, like his Holy-Rolling and the foolishness about being born again — my dad always said, “Well, if he had to be born again, why would he choose to be born again as Jimmy Carter?” — gave pause to a lot of northern liberal Democrats, especially Jews. I think a crucial moment in this was when the Atlanta civil rights establishment, which is where all the major non-civil-rights organizations were located, went out of their way to go all around the country to sell Carter to the liberal wing of the Democratic Party as a new kind of liberal. And what this new kind of liberal was, ultimately, was a white Southern Democrat racial liberal. And as I think more and more about it, I think that’s the moment when we can see the sign of identitarian leftism beginning to displace the vestiges, or really the residues, of the old trade-union, working-class-based Democratic coalition. The New Left’s Legacy Melissa Naschek What do the two of you see as the legacy of the New Left? Adolph Reed I think it’s complicated. Most of the current leadership in AFL-CIO are people who have either direct or indirect connections to the New Left. That’s one of the reasons why I think this contention that the labor movement has to atone for its horrible history of sexism and racism and stuff like that is ridiculous, because all those people have been dead for a long time. And women and blacks and other non-white minorities are overrepresented among the membership of the labor movement compared to the general population. This is kind of parochial, but I’m also part of the cliché that people who came out of the Left went into the academy . And within political science, and some of the other social science disciplines too, when we found that there were big enough clusters of us holding down professorships or aspiring to professorships, it made both natural career sense and natural political sense, given our objective position, to work to make Marxism respectable in the formal academy. And I’ll say parenthetically that I’m always fearful when the political sense and the career sense converge, because it’s so easy to bullsh-t yourself. That’s the easiest thing in the world to do. But while there were some overtures from the political science and sociology mainstreams back in the day — not economics, of course, because that’s just divinity school — what turned out to be the case was that the price of intellectual respectability from one’s colleagues was breaking with an epistemic understanding of Marx’s eleventh thesis on [Ludwig] Feuerbach. Vivek Chibber The one that said, “Philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point, however, is to change it.” Adolph Reed Right, which people sometimes think of as a moral injunction. But more significantly, and I think this is one of the things that separates Marxists from non-Marxists in my view, that the intellectual foundation of the way through which we see the world rests on the principle of commitment to class struggle. And by that I don’t mean practicing at the barricades but an understanding that the world is most fundamentally moving according to the logic of Marxism. Melissa Naschek Well, also the idea that your intellectual work should actually be useful for people who are trying to do politics. Adolph Reed God forbid, right? And so structuralist Marxism emerged as a kind of halfway house for the Althusserians and some of the people around the New Left Review and stuff like that. And as sites of resistance began to atrophy outside the university, there was no basis for this epistemic principle unless you brought it with you, that the world moves by contradiction and has to change. In a moment when the ruling class’s power is greater than it’s ever been, and there are fewer and fewer real sources of opposition coming from outside the academy, many decided to take this ride. And so, for many of these radicals, the next thing they know, they were simply just structuralists. And it seems to me that the difference between a structural Marxist and a structuralist recedes toward zero, and all both of them could do was predict that things were going to keep getting worse. And it’s at that point when the better ones among them settle into a genteel alcoholism or coach their kids soccer teams or grow their gardens. And the worst of them did a lot worse. At the same time, it’s also true that within the academy — and this is probably more true in the history departments than in some other fields — as the disciplines democratized, the center of gravity of academic work began to expand more broadly. Wouldn’t you agree, Vivek? Vivek Chibber Yeah, absolutely. My sense is that, if I follow the same sequence of analysis as Adolph, I would say that the legacy of the New Left can be appreciated in two different domains. One is a broader culture and one is intellectual and academic. In the broader culture, I think there are a lot of positive legacies of the New Left, because of the antiwar and civil rights movements. Although, I’m not sure I want to call the civil rights movement New Left per se. I think of the civil rights movement as the last stage of the older left, because the key coterie around Martin Luther King Jr, such as A. Philip Randolph, Bayard Rustin , Tom Kahn, and Stanley Levison, were — not just generationally, but also ideologically — old-style socialists. They weren’t counterculture socialists. Nevertheless, civil rights is identified with the New Left, and it’s also true that a lot of the Freedom Riders and the students were the ones who joined the New Left. The civil rights movement had a profoundly positive influence on the culture in pushing it toward a kind of instinctive anti-racism and cosmopolitanism, and then the Vietnam War movement had yet another huge impact on that. What was the essence of the antiwar movement? It was the recognition that the Vietnamese are no less human than the Americans, and that their dignity, rights, and autonomy have to be respected. And this was also the last moment of the great independence movements in Africa as well, which had a gigantic impact on the academy and the culture more broadly. My mother came to this country right in the last stages of the Vietnam War, and she can attest to the differences from the 1970s to now as the positive elements of that antiwar movement seeped in. So while it’s true that a lot of the packaging of the 1960s is now the hippies and the counterculture and all that, the positive impact of all of those movements supporting independence and opposing imperialism, alongside the civil rights movement, injected a dose of cosmopolitanism and, in a very positive sense, multiculturalism, that is not to be denigrated and is very important. Then, however, there is the intellectual legacy of that moment and the political legacy in a more narrow sense, which is: How do we conceive of politics and social change? I think this is largely negative. It’s the aging New Left that created this new form of radicalism, which at best is sort of indifferent to working people but at worst is openly contemptuous toward them. And it crafted a vision of political change that is very narrowly conceived around the material interests and the frustrated ambitions of, as Adolph just said, this shifting center of gravity within the professional classes, away from old white men and toward these upwardly mobile women and minorities who do great for themselves, but find that they’re still not given all the goodies that the older white men are given. And instead of recognizing this as simply a kind of frustrated bourgeois politics, the New Leftists said “No, this is radical power.” I think this is mistaken and had a very negative impact. As part of that intellectual legacy, we got all the various alphabet soup “posties”: postcolonialism, postmodernism, poststructuralism. Whereas Marxism was once the theory of people who call themselves radical, these replaced it. And it’s not just that they’ve been a blight upon intellectual life. They are, I think, the most obvious and glaring example of the cultural and moral degeneration of the neoliberal era. But now, here’s the saving grace. That, even just in my own lifetime, the intellectual resources to criticize a lot of this intellectual detritus was also created by the New Left. I think the New Left put economics on a footing that it had never been before within the Left. I think the moral and philosophical underpinnings of socialism are a lot stronger than they used to be. There is a huge corpus of left-inspired historiography of race and colonialism that we now have thanks to them, and that, despite the packaging that the postcolonialists and the postmodernists later put on it, actually shows people’s struggles were the same everywhere. The goals were the same everywhere and the convergence around a similar set of interests was the same everywhere. This all came out of the New Left. So the legacy is mixed in the following sense. The momentum of the last ten years has been horrible, as the Left is trying to recover itself, and that negative momentum all comes out of the direct creation of the New Left as it aged and kind of sh-t on the world as it was leaving the scene. But the intellectual resources to do something and to criticize that also come out of that project. And my view is we need to recapture the moral and cultural commitments of the older left but build on the intellectual resources that the newer left has given us. Adolph Reed Sounds right to me. Well put. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Socialism Deferred: The Communist Party of Italy and the Historic Compromise of 1976
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: American politics is at a crossroads. All that was once considered certain or possible is now in question. For the first time since the early 20th century, American Socialists are gaining considerable municipal and state level influence through successful and highly publicized electoral campaigns. After a largely successful midterm showing, the DSA established itself as a small but potent force in American politics. For the first time there is a comparatively large cohort of elected DSA members holding local, state, and federal office. Along with this heightened political influence comes greater political risk. Questions of electoral positioning and maneuver take on greater weight. Examining the past experience of socialist and non-socialist alliances can be instructive. Italy provides a pertinent example of a large socialist party, the Italian Communist Party (PCI), that entered an election in 1976 that seemed to have it poised on the precipice of entering government for the first time since the onset of the cold war. This did not occur. Instead, it offers an example of the critical importance of electoral strategy, social research, and ideological flexibility. Despite a major electoral breakthrough with a historic 34% of the vote in 1976, the Italian Communist Party (PCI) was unable to translate this into a wider challenge to the institutional and economic order in Italy. The Communist Party benefitted from the leadership of Chairman Enrico Berlinguer, widely recognized as a particularly charismatic and talented politician. He and his associates pursued a strategic alliance with the Christian Democrats known as the Historic Compromise to bolster future electoral efforts. In reality the compromise undermined the long-term viability of the PCI project. Its failure stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of the mandate delivered by voters as well as a failure to anticipate the political realities of being a subordinate non-governing party to the Christian Democrats. At no point did the DC share power with the PCI. The party agreed initially to a non-sfiducia regime, meaning it promised not to call for a vote of no confidence. Ultimately, the PCI endorsed the government under long-serving and known conservative Christian Democratic Prime Minister Giuliio Andreotti in 1978 even though the party was denied any ministerial positions. Transitioning from the no-confidence regime to the “National Solidarity Government” the PCI still did not receive a meaningful stake in national power. Forced to defend unpopular measures, it ultimately entered the next election of 1979 in a worse position, presaging a process of decline throughout the 1980s and ultimate dissolution in 1991. the cold war dilemma of the pci The Italian Communist Party in 1976 was a mass based electoral Socialist Party confronted by the harsh political realities of the Cold War. It was viewed by many in the center and on the right as an agent of Moscow, functioning to subvert the democratic order. Simultaneously, to many Italian workers, peasants, and increasingly large shares of the petty bourgeoisie as well as students, the Italian Communist Party was a vehicle to advance democratic struggles that ranged from the armed resistance to Fascism to the right to divorce. Berlinguer and the leadership of the PCI correctly viewed their reliance on the Soviet Union as an obstacle to the democratic transfer of power. They formulated a new political line to demonstrate that the Party was a responsible democratic institution while also remaining faithful to the class struggle. Having its foundation in longserving leader of the Party and prominent Communist International Official, Palmiro Togliatti’s, recognition of Parliament as a legitimate vehicle for class struggle and his belief that there were multiple national roads to socialism, the line adopted by the PCI came to be known as “Eurocommunism” (a view adopted in different ways by the French, Spanish, and Italian Communist parties). Eurocommunism revolved around the idea that it was possible to utilize the parliament of bourgeois republics to peacefully transition from capitalism to socialism. This perspective tied all three parties (though the French would eventually break with Eurocommunism) to electoralism. This raises a basic problem: how does one retain the revolutionary goals and impetus of Socialism while supporting a bourgeois electoral process? The ideological basis of the Historic Compromise was established by Berlinguer in a series of articles released in the main party newspaper and official organ, Rinascita. Berlinguer was starting from a position of perennial opposition to not only the DC, but the entire spectrum of “bourgeois ideology”. To accomplish the ideological shift, he separated, in line with Italian historic experience, anti-Imperialism from absolute anticapitalism: “It is the duty of communists and all who fight for the cause of democratic progress and of the liberation of the people to raise the level of consciousness regarding these truths, in order to direct vigilant attention to all of the threats that imperialism and the ruling bourgeois class poses to the freedom of people and independence of nations.” (1) This opened the line of reasoning that would allow a Party militant or longtime supporter to consider that the cause of democratic progress writ large may constitute sufficient ideological similarity to the Communist commitment to anti-Fascism, thus to allow for the Communists to stand in alliance. This was not sufficient, however. To confront decades of inherited bias against accommodation with the DC, Berlinguer sought to employ one of the most potent symbols of the PCI, the Resistenza. Referencing the Salerno Turn when the Kingdom of Italy joined the Allies in World War Two through an agreement of all of the Anti-Fascist forces in the country, he wrote, “The more profound sense of the turn (at Salerno) was the necessity and the desire of the Communist Party to come to terms with all of Italian history, and with all of the historic forces (Socialists, Catholics, and others with democratic inspirations) who were present on the national scene and who fought alongside us for democracy, for national independence, and unity.” (2) By invoking the broad anti-fascist front of wartime, he was suggesting it might be reconstituted in the present. Berlinguer concluded, “If it is true that a democratic renewal can only be realized if it is supported by vast majority of the population, there is not only a need for a policy of large social alliances but also a determined system of political agreements that fosters a convergence and collaboration between all of democratic and popular forces until there is realized a political alliance among them.” (3) This justified the fundamental political logic of the historic compromise, that it was acceptable for the PCI to explore uniting with non-Communist forces to oppose Imperialism, that there were historic forces in the country (Socialism, Catholics, others) who could be united with today because of their role in the historic anti-fascist struggle, and that a revolutionary democratic program can only be pursued through a system of large social and political alliances. What Berlinguer did not anticipate was that the convergence he spoke of would lead voters toward the DC, not the PCI. the irony of the historic compromise Not only was the PCI suddenly forced to defend, in the name of the Historic Compromise, unpopular government policies such as the partial elimination of the scala mobile, rising costs of living due to inflationary monetary policy, and a partial dismantling of the gains earned by the unions during the previous round of labor militancy; it also faced internal dissatisfaction. There was widespread confusion among the Party: “From the start, much of the PCI membership was surprised and confused by the historic compromise; many were jolted when the leadership proposed an alliance with a political force that had been seen as the enemy for so long.” (4) According to Lucio Magri, author of the Tailor of Ulm and one of the founders of Manifesto, a leftwing journal that split from and ultimately rejoined the PCI, “If anything, younger and more combative sections of the population, less accustomed to discipline and delegation, wanted to participate in decision-making and to see the results sooner rather than later.” (5) This internal confusion was aggravated following the election because, “The PCI constituencies expected the party to use its leverage to push through far-reaching reforms. Instead the leadership devoted all its efforts to working out a formal agreement with the DC, backing down on major issues to keep negotiations going…the DC passed a series of measures that served its own interests…raising prices for the basic consumer goods, public transportation, and utilities; and dismantling the cost of living escalator mechanism (scala mobile), which protected the organized working class against inflation.” (6) Here were the perils of being a junior coalition partner. The PCI was not in government but because of the Historic Compromise was forced to defend policies that undermined its own position among its constituents in the name of a broader goal: namely, to demonstrate its “fitness” to govern. Even those elements within the Party that supported the Historic Compromise, according to Magri, were expecting reform but received only defence of the status quo, “Even those convinced of the rightness of Berlinguer’s project not only hoped for but willed a profound change in economic and social policy, and in Italy’s international position, mode of governance and distribution of power. A compromise maybe – but not subaltern cohabitation.” (7) the road not taken Was this the only path available to Berlinguer? Some both on the left and among disinterested historians saw another potential avenue that could have been pursued but was not explored; a Left Unity Coalition between the PCI and the Italian Socialist Party (PSI) – and smaller Left parties. An effective electoral coalition depended both on ideological unity and a program focused on the desires of the PCI base; namely, defense of the scala mobile and living standards of the popular classes, and an end to the corruption identified as a by-product of DC rule. Both the PCI and the official newspaper of the Italian Socialist Party, Avanti, regularly called out the corruption of the DC. The prospective coalition would also have entailed a defense of NATO, but with a varied foreign policy that at times would have been at odds with the NATO’a wider positions, for example, leaning on traditionally good relations between Italy and the Arab Republics. (8) Historian Paul Ginsborg notes that “…the country was crying out for change and reform. It would not be possible to achieve either by making an alliance with the DC. Berlinguer, it is argued, should have capitalized upon the enduring movement of protest in civil society in order to forge an alternative to Christian Democrat politics entirely.” (9) The PCI could not have taken power immediately, but it could have used the years after 1976 to build a united opposition, and to prepare the terrain for a decisive victory at the next elections.” (10) This suggests a qualitatively different view of the potential for the democratic transition in a bourgeois republic. While it was not realistic for a Left Coalition to assume power in 1976, the process of unity coalition building could have served as a vehicle for the consolidation of the Left into a more viable alternative pole in Italian politics. Nor did the PSI represent the only available alliance partner. There was as well the New Left which existed in various forms, ultimately to be joined by the explosive mixture of new social actors and popular demands that emerged on the scene with the Movement of ‘77. the italian new left To the Left of the PCI was a nebulous group organized around a handful of prominent thinkers such as Mario Tronti, Antonio Negri, and Silvia Federici. While their positions can be considered generally Left, they varied significantly on who or what constituted the proletarian class or revolutionary subject. Loosely, they agreed upon a broad conception of politics that placed the organization of the working class as something to be pursued outside of the boundaries of established organizations such as existing trade unions and the Communist or Socialist Parties. For this reason they adopted “Autonomia” (Autonomy) as the label for a body of wide ranging Marxist thought. Alongside this creative application of Marxism were numerous other ideological projects that embraced a variety of ideologies and identities; together they occupied a nebulous space best defined as the “New Left”. While there were numerous periodicals and journals such as Potere Operaio, Primo Maggio, Quaderni Rossi, etc. that all expressed different currents of thought to the left of the PCI, we can view the New Left coalition party, Proletarian Democracy (DP) as the primary organization in question, at least with regards to electoral matters. In the 1976 election the party received approximately 550,000 votes which earned it 6 Members of Parliament. (11) While not decisive, they represented a viable left-wing ally that when taken together with the Socialists at 9% would have allowed for the emergence of a Left Coalition in Parliament that the DC would have had to accommodate in some fashion, even as broader ideological unity was explored. The PCI’s refusal to engage with the New Left could be understood as a combination of old sectarianism and a fundamental misunderstanding or inability to recognize the new insurgent populations that defined the New Left. It is no coincidence that only several months later, after the elections, the Movement of ‘77 exploded onto the scene of Italian politics, expressing many different tendencies and modes of thought, but overall frustration with the existing political status quo, including the PCI. Magri summarizes the composition of the Movement of ‘77: “It was mainly a protest movement in a period of general downturn, mostly driven by anger and disappointment, and kindling huge hopes for a new world…its social base was new and heterogeneous: various marginal groups (unemployed youth, rank and file union activists in the railway and health sectors, jobless graduates), clustered together, or tried to cluster, around the students, whereas industrial workers were neither much in evidence nor the class centrally at issue in the protests.” (12) Clearly, this heterogeneous movement was far from being composed of the PCI’s traditional base, that is the industrial working class. But it represented exactly the constituency for a broader Left alliance against the Center and Right. It could be seen then that the failure of the PCI to extend a meaningful hand to the New Left for the Election of 1976 was a profound error. The Party’s aversion to ideological compromise, its unwillingness to cede ideological and organizational control of the coalition, was fatal. Of course, it also reflected the Party’s opportunism in seeking to secure a grand alliance with the DC. the politics of the possible Was the Left Unity Coalition realistic? The experience of the prodigal Manifesto group which had split from the PCI in the 1960s to form an independent Marxist journal and returned by the late 1970s and the Proletarian Unity Party for Communism which experienced a similar trajectory, both demonstrate that small ideologically left dissident factions were able to dissolve and return to the PCI proper. This suggests a degree of underlying compatibility. Ironically the PCI by refusing to pursue a meaningful alliance with the wider forces of the left contradicted Togliatti’s own thoughts regarding parliament, “In the second place, it is necessary for the parties that fight for socialism, and the communist parties in the front rank of them, to be strong, numerous, well organised and for them to know how to work and fight in such a way as to win a decisive influence in the decisive strata of the working class and the people. In the third place, it is necessary for these parties to be united in their action, because this not only increases their numerical weight…but can allow them to establish a reciprocal understanding and a collaboration with those political forces that are not hostile to social reforms of a socialist type and to a consequent policy of peace.” (13) Furthermore, had the PCI been basing their perception of the role of parliament in 1976 on the broad call for democratic unity advanced by Togliatti – following the logic of the Historic Compromise itself – the unity of the PCI, PSI, DP, and Italian Social Democratic Party (PSDI) could have been pursued under the wide umbrella of anti-imperialism and in defense of democratic values. There also existed a degree of popular support for this position, reported in Avanti.. A press conference of neighborhood leaders appearing in the Party’s official organ indicated that there also was a degree of PSI support for a broader understanding of the left. (14) The Socialist leadership around De Martino could have been approached by the PCI to draft a new unity program to create an alternative center-left coalition. Martino himself advanced a lukewarm but open position at the PSI party congress of 1976, stating in his address to the Party that it was critical that the PSI consider a left-wing alternative politics and observed that some elements within the Party were insisting that the PSI declare they would not join any government without the PCI. (15) While retaining a desire for autonomy and flexibility going into the election, De Martino recognized that the primary strategic goal of the PSI was, “to build a leftwing alliance and alternative.” The failure of the PCI then is not that it rejected an immediate electoral alternative based on alliance with the PSI, but that it did not, after the election, devote energy to constructing a long-term autonomous left alliance that could in time replace the DC. The difficulties in synthesizing a Left Unity Coalition among the PCI, PSI, New Left, and Others were significant. They represented notable differences in viewpoints regarding many issues. However, given the growing popular dissatisfaction with the DC, historic inter-party relations particularly between the PCI and PSI was not impossible. Ginsborg highlights that, while difficult, the decision to not pursue a Left-Unity Coalition would have fateful consequences as, “In the summer of 1976 the opportunity, albeit fraught with difficulty, existed for building an alternative to the Christian Democrats. The opportunity was not taken, and no such chance was to present itself again. the italian lesson What does the Italian General Election of 1976 teach us about the potential rise of Socialist Governance in the United States in the wake of the 2026 Midterm Elections? The 2026 Midterms are not the Italian General Election in 1976. Unlike the PCI which was a well organized, disciplined, national political force, the DSA is still a pre-party formation employing primarily democratic electoral infrastructure to contest specific races. While the PCI could rely upon professional cadre to coordinate national efforts, the DSA is composed primarily of volunteers. Like the General Elections in 1976 Italy, the DSA has made a tremendous breakthrough, relatively speaking, with six candidates being elected to federal office and numerous downballot or endorsed victories. (16) Despite this success, the DSA remains fundamentally subordinate to the Democratic Party. Because of the need to oppose the Republican Party and the still relatively marginal position of the Socialist Movement in the USA, the DSA like the PCI, is compelled to support policy packages pushed by the Democrats that are fundamentally antithetical to a Socialist vision for the United States. But the DSA may suffer should their bourgeois partners, who constitute the actual power in government, pursue policies that undermine the DSA. To combat the effect of being tied to a larger bourgeois force, the DSA must expand its political imagination which the PCI refused to do. It is imperative that socialists seize the mandate offered by voters and propose meaningful reforms to meet immediate material expectations. Simultaneously, it is possible to begin an ideological process of Left Coalition Building which may mean that while a still marginal force in 2026, the DSA enters 2028 and beyond as an independent political party capable of advancing the socialist project and vision that motivates its membership. To speak of coalition building is also to highlight the stark difference between the possibilities open to the PCI that do not exist in the same measure for DSA. Unfortunately, there are no comparably sized overtly Socialist parties that the DSA can join hands with to create the beginning of a coalition. That said, there are options the DSA can cultivate. Third parties such as the Greens, Working Families Party, and others who are not explicitly Socialist could unite with the DSA in a Popular Democratic Coalition; or at least on specific initiatives like the Green New Deal or Cost of Living, that might prepare the ground for later and broader convergence. Similarly there is the possibility of establishing an explicitly political alliance with progressive and independent elements of organized labor. This would be distinct from the broad imperative of supporting the unions as vehicles for securing tangible gains for working people and would represent an effort to create a specific political project transitioning from solely economic initiatives towards broader related challenges. Progressive Democrats are seemingly a potential coalition partner but represent an acute danger for the DSA. They are exactly the mechanism by which the DSA can be maneuvered into supporting candidates and policies that undermine the position of the DSA which could include continued support for Zionism, continued “legal” deportations, or continued funding for foreign wars. That said, Progressive Democrats could be persuaded to provide indirect material support for the DSA by channeling funds and resources to DSA initiatives. This does not amount to joining a formal Popular Democratic Coalition, but nonetheless could help. The common thread running through all of these options is the necessity for the Popular Democratic Coalition to have a specific end goal in mind. Unity for the sake of unity was not viable nor beneficial for the PCI nor would it be viable for the DSA.
